Photograph: Nonoy Lacson/Reuters View image in fullscreen Ateneo de Zamboanga University after a shooting that killed two people in Zamboanga on Tuesday. Photograph: Nonoy Lacson/Reuters Philippines Philippine school shooter kills fellow student and himself in livestreamed attack Country’s second fatal school shooting in two months took place in southern city of ⁠Zamboanga Natasha May and agencies Tue 18 Aug 2026 09.21 EDT First published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 00.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A student livestreamed himself shooting and killing another pupil in a classroom in the southern Philippines before taking his own ⁠life, ​the second school attack in the country in less than two months. The shooting took ⁠place at a school attached to Ateneo de Zamboanga University in the southern city of ⁠Zamboanga, a Catholic private institution in western Mindanao. Zamboanga city’s mayor, Khymer Adan Olaso, told the DZMM radio station that the ‌shooter “managed to enter carrying a high-powered firearm and a .45-calibre pistol”. Philippines blocks GoreBox gaming app after school shooting kills three Read more The interior secretary, Victor Remulla, confirmed the ninth-grade suspect had livestreamed the attack on social media. The shooter’s Facebook account has since been disabled. In the video, which was circulated by local media, the barrel of a gun is seen moving down a hallway before it is pointed into a classroom and fired. Children in school uniforms are seen screaming and rushing for an exit. National police are now trying to “establish the motive behind the shooting, determine the ownership and source of the firearm used, and find out how it was brought inside the school campus”, the interior ministry said. Hours later, the Philippines’ customs department said it had ordered the “preventive suspension” of an agent who owned the guns “allegedly used by the student involved”. The customs deputy chief of staff, Noel Bendijo, told AFP that customs staff had acted on intelligence from their own officers in Zamboanga. “The information is that he was the father of [the alleged shooter] … As for the actual firearms used and how the kid was able to access them, all of those are still under investigation,” he said. “We’ve also spoken with the party involved. He understands but of course he’s also grieving because he also lost his child. That’s a nightmare for any parent.” View image in fullscreen Philippine police gather at the school in Zamboanga after the shooting. Photograph: Roel Parreno/AFP/Getty Images Police when asked about the customs report said only that they were still investigating. The Philippine president, Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr, said in an online post: “We grieve with the families and the entire [school] community over a tragedy that should never have happened. I have directed our law enforcement agencies to conduct a thorough investigation into this incident and to determine what more must be done to prevent another family, another school and another community from suffering the same grief.” In June at a public high school in Tacloban City, three students were killed and about 20 injured after two students opened fire on campus. In response, the government banned an online game , Gorebox, after it was discovered that at least one of the alleged shooters regularly played it, and reopened a senate inquiry on child safety in digital spaces. The department of education told a separate senate committee last month that more support was needed to prevent a “copycat phenomenon”, as more incidents of violence followed the shooting, including bomb threats, stabbing and the recovery of firearms and ammunition, local media reported. South-east Asia is grappling with violence among secondary school students, with a 14-year-old boy in Thailand allegedly shooting his grandparents and then killing more people at his school earlier this month before turning the gun on ⁠himself. Nine people died, including the shooter, teachers and a 12-year-old girl , and more than 30 were wounded. https://www.perthnow.com.au/news/disaste.text: The European Union has deployed three helicopters and two water bomber aircraft to tackle Belgium's biggest wildfire on record, as local authorities told residents in some villages to leave their homes. The blaze in the High Fens, a nature reserve in the east of the country, has been burning since Friday and firefighters from across Belgium and neighbouring Germany and Luxembourg have sought to contain it, as have the army and farmers. By early Sunday AEST, it had burned 2700ha, the office of the governor of Liege said, indicating the fire was spreading, having increased from 1600 hectares earlier in the day. That makes the fire by far the biggest on record in Belgium — nearly double the size of a blaze in 2011 that burned close to 1400ha, data from the European Forest Fire Information System showed. Local authorities asked residents of several villages to evacuate their homes as a precaution on Saturday, due to changing winds and smoke in the area. Tourists staying in the area were advised to leave, while a children's summer camp was also evacuated, Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken said in a post on X. The terrain of the nature reserve was making it difficult for emergency services to attack the fire at close range using their usual resources, the Liege governor's office noted. European countries including Belgium suffered their fifth heatwave of the summer this week. Scientists say human-caused climate change has increased the likelihood of the hot and dry conditions that allow wildfires to spread faster and burn longer. The EU co-ordinates the deployment of extra resources pooled from European countries, when a country requests emergency help. The aircraft sent to Belgium on Saturday were from the Czech Republic, Sweden and the Netherlands, EU Crisis Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said in a post on X. Meanwhile, local officials said 650 residents evacuated their homes as a wildfire burned in Landes, south-western France. The fire began on Thursday and, according to authorities, reignited on Saturday - with more than 500 firefighters deployed to tackle the blaze.

(REUTERS/Marko Djurica) BELGRADE Reuters) — The European Union’s Civil Protection Mechanism sent helicopters and firefighters to help Serbia fight a massive wildfire in a nature reserve in the northeast of the country, the head of the EU mission to Belgrade said on Saturday. Serbia activated the mechanism on Friday after struggling for weeks with a wildfire in Deliblatska Pescara, a unique mixture of sand dunes and woods about 80 km (50 miles) from the capital Belgrade, as well as other blazes in the southwest of the country. “We stand with Serbia in protecting lives, livelihoods and the unique natural heritage of Deliblatska Sands,” Andreas Beckerath, the head of the EU mission to Belgrade, wrote on X. Luka Causic, the head of the Serbian Department for Emergencies, said that European aid consists of four Black Hawk firefighting helicopters from Romania, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, 55 firefighters and 24 vehicles from Germany, and 69 firefighters and 15 vehicles from Romania. One helicopter from Romania and one from Slovakia joined firefighting efforts on Saturday, while two others from the Czech Republic will be engaged on Sunday, Serbia’s Interior Ministry said in a statement. Romanian firefighters and vehicles have also arrived in the town od Bela Crkva, near the fire. A German team is expected to arrive on August 24, it said. Serbia is not a member of the EU but has access to emergency EU help under its Civil Protection Mechanism. This summer, Belgrade sent a firefighting helicopter and emergency response team to help Spain combat wildfires after repeated blazes across Europe sapped EU resources. A Russian Emergencies Ministry IL-76P firefighting plane landed in the southern Serbian city of Nis on Wednesday to tackle the Deliblatska Pescara wildfire, which has gutted thousands of hectares of pine forest since late July. Causic said the situation was more stable on Saturday, but that strong winds were expected and the priority is to protect settlements and human lives. Other major wildfires were also active in the rugged Stolovi mountain range in the southwest of the country. In neighbouring North Macedonia, a major wildfire was raging in the municipality of Strumica, south of the capital Skopje. https://www.dw.com/en/five-women-killed-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PnSc Prefer DW on Google The UN report noted that women often face barriers to accessing the justice system Image: Ihsaan Haffejee/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO Advertisement Around 47,000 women and girls — or five every hour — were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025, according to a United Nations report released on Tuesday. This figure equates to around 60% of women and girls who were victims of intentional homicides last year, the report said ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25. The total fatalities were calculated based on statistics from 122 countries and territories. They translate to an average of 129 women and girls killed by their close social circle each day. Africa recorded the highest number of femicides , at 22,100. Asia followed, with 15,100 victims, ahead of the Americas with 7,400, Europe with 2,100 and Oceania with 300. Femicide is a hate crime broadly defined as "the intentional killing of women or girls because they are female." Why so many women fear for their lives in South Africa To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video One in three women experienced physical or sexual violence The report also found that although global homicide rates have declined, femicide rates have fallen at a slower pace, particularly in the Americas and Europe. According to the UN, this shows the barriers women often face in accessing the justice system and that "these crimes are deeply rooted in social norms and gender stereotypes." Nearly one in three women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence, yet only 7% reported it to the police, a separate UN Women report found. According to estimates by UN Women and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC, the number of women and girls killed by a family member or an intimate partner has wavered between 45,000 and 51,000 over the past several years. Gang warfare in Ecuador fuels wave of femicides To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Frightening attitudes, social norms, and the failure of institutional safeguards create an environment in which killing a wife, daughter, mother, or sister becomes 'tolerable,'" UNODC director Monica Juma said. "Changing this reality calls for sustained action across all levels of society." Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, said that the world needed to "act urgently to ensure no warning sign is ignored, no survivor is left without protection, and no perpetrator escapes accountability."
